prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a concrete discovery-plus-invention of the kind the committee can state in one sentence: Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes light-shift and motional errors, and Ye's group took the strontium clock to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. The result is unambiguous and has been reproduced independently by many national laboratories. It already feeds tests of fundamental constants and relativity, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second. The two-name credit is compact and matches the credit that all eight members proposed in the opening ballots. It is also the only shortlisted candidate that all eight members ranked, and four of us placed it first or second, so the support does not depend on one subfield. I treat that breadth only as a cross-check on the scientific arguments, which stand on their own.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that lattice clocks sit on top of already-honoured work: Hall and Haensch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, ion control) cover neighbouring ground, and ion clocks are a competing line with comparable accuracy. A prize here could be read as honouring a record in precision rather than a new phenomenon. Other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Bloom/Ludlow, Hinkley) are outside the credit, and Ye's contribution is partly many-body clock physics and comb-linked comparison. If the SI second is redefined only later, some would argue the committee should wait for that milestone.

responses.point: Kroll ranked lattice clocks first because magic-wavelength trapping opens a new regime of measurement, with 1e-18 uncertainty, redefinition of the second and geodesy as consequences, and finds the two-name credit clean.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the credit. I would add that the discovery side, not only the metrology, is what makes this a physics prize: it is a clear measurable outcome that tests the constancy of nature's parameters. Where I differ slightly is on timing. Kroll reads recognition as timely or overdue. I read it as timely but not urgent, so I do not think the committee should treat the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to rush.

responses.point: Pearce ranked IceCube first, arguing that a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux and its source associations opened a new observational window, and that Halzen, Karle and Spiering are a fair three-person credit.
responses.response: I share the view that this is a real discovery. I ranked it third in my own opening list and it is my first alternative from the astroparticle side. My reservation is attribution and maturity. The flux is robust, but the sources of most of the neutrinos are unresolved, and the credit relative to AMANDA and Baikal and to a roughly 300-member collaboration is hard to isolate. Single-name leadership roles are not the same as discovery credit, so I would want a clearer argument for why these three are the discoverers before ranking this above the clocks. I do not find that argument yet, and I would not call it a flaw in the ballot, just an unfinished case.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked lattice clocks first and topological insulators second, calling the latter mature and overdue and the former timely with a stable interpretation.
responses.response: On the clocks we agree. On topological insulators, I ranked them lower in my opening list than she did because the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions overlaps in concept and because the credit is contested between Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Molenkamp and Hasan. Her argument for maturity is persuasive, and the ballot has the broadest top-three support. I therefore name B053 as an alternative. I still do not think breadth of opening support should decide between the two. The attribution problem there is harder than in the clock case.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked optical lattice clocks only fourth, placing tunnel magnetoresistance, DMFT and topological insulators above them, and noted that the clock credit overlaps with earlier comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: That overlap is real, and I list it as my main reservation. I do not think it is disqualifying. The 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured a comb technique and the manipulation of single ions, while the lattice clock is a different idea, trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, with a different outcome. Eriksson's own top candidates were not shortlisted in this round, so I cannot compare them directly. Among those that are here, I would ask him which of them he thinks beats the clocks on clarity of discovery and attribution.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first as the architecture behind superconducting quantum processors, with Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf as a natural theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: The trio is natural, and the physics is important. My concern is timing and overlap. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits sits next to it, and the technology is still moving, so some of the credit may look different after fault-tolerance milestones. Compared with the clocks, the stable, independently verified performance figure is less sharp here. I do not rank circuit QED above the clocks, but I see it as a serious later candidate.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give to the earlier prizes for combs (2005) and ion control (2012) when judging novelty of the lattice clock.
Whether Ye's contribution is best credited as accuracy and stability records or as the broader many-body clock programme, and whether other lattice-clock groups deserve credit.
Whether B053 should be considered the stronger case once the credit allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan and the overlap with the 2016 prize are examined.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second should affect the timing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. None of the credited names on the shortlisted ballots is my PhD supervisor (Gross), early mentor (Rubinstein), frequent co-author (Van Riet) or part of the Uppsala theoretical-physics group. I am a string theorist and cosmologist, so I am not an expert in precision atomic physics and rely on the opening evidence.
